about: Every Porchsite release, newest first. cloudflare/scripts/downloads.sh refuses to build a release that has no entry here and publishes this file as /changelog.json, /changelog/ and in latest.json. Per release: release (its id, <UTC date>-<commit>), date, security (true: it fixes something an attacker could use; update soon), reconnect (true: the assistant tool list changed; remove and re-add the site's connector), migrations (the Cloudflare edition's new migration files; the server edition applies its own schema on start), changes (2-6 plain lines an assistant can read to the owner). Write the entry before building: the release id is today's UTC date and the commit being built (git rev-parse --short HEAD); commit this file after the build.

changes: The deep site check on large listing sites is cheaper again: it only prepares the text of entries a checked page actually shows.

The deep site check now finishes on large listing sites: it stops as soon as every page is shown to be reachable instead of crawling up to 200 pages and giving up, and it costs a fraction of the time.
After you recover your site with your recovery code, you now see the readers who can still sign in, each with a Remove button, so a reader added from a lost or stolen device can be cut off at once.
Prepared copies (off unless you turn them on) are now much cheaper to serve: a stored page is handed out after one quick check, so a new visitor anywhere skips the full build.
Names with underscores, like theme_create, now read normally in the Markdown copies of your pages.
A malformed archive filter with a hidden line break is refused the same way on both editions.
An agent reading your site no longer gets a spurious "out of date" error when its read happens to cross a minute boundary; the site rebuilds the answer once and replies.
Updated the build tools behind the scenes; the site itself is unchanged.
A page's first view reads the database 5 times instead of 11, and dates are worked out once per page, so pages are cheaper to build.
The Markdown copies of your pages no longer put backslashes before ordinary punctuation, so agents can read and copy them as written; anything that could change the meaning is still escaped.
A visitor or agent coming back to a page that hasn't changed gets a quick "not changed" reply all day, not only within the same minute, so the page isn't rebuilt.
Pages that show time-based details (opening hours, notices, event dates) still switch at exactly the right moment in your site's time zone, including daylight-saving changes.
An agent you've signed in as yourself (for example in your own browser) can now read your review pages, drafts and previews as plain text instead of picking through the page.
Passwords, passkeys, invitations, keys and one-time links are never included, and these copies are never stored anywhere.
Your own writing in drafts is clearly marked as your words, so an agent reads it as content, not as instructions to follow.
Pages that list entries (the home page, streams, the Markdown copies) are about a third cheaper to build: an entry's full text is only prepared when the page actually shows it.
Viewing a page never writes to the database any more; picture sizes are worked out when a picture is uploaded.
/llms.txt no longer puts backslashes in front of ordinary punctuation, so agents read it as plain text.
Agents you trust can now read your site, including a private one, without being able to change anything: make a read-only key under Assistants and give it to the agent.
New lighter tools for agents: read one published page, list pages by stream, tag or date, and search, instead of downloading the whole site.
On a private site, an agent with a read key gets the same pages and Markdown copies a visitor would; without a key it sees only the sign-in page. Revoking a key cuts it off at once.
Reconnect your assistant once after updating so it sees the new tools.
Pages are much cheaper to serve, so sites stay within Cloudflare's free plan: a visitor or agent whose copy is current gets a quick "not changed" reply without the page being rebuilt.
Missing pages get a small plain "not found" reply instead of a full themed page when the address doesn't look like a page.
/llms.txt is built from page titles and summaries instead of rendering every page, so it loads in a fraction of the time.
Agent visit counts are now gathered in memory and saved about once a minute; a few visits may go uncounted if a server restarts.
Self-hosted sites behind a web server that handles https work again; the previous release wrongly redirected their own internal requests.
Visiting your site with http:// now takes you to the secure https:// address instead of showing an error page.
On a private site, anyone who isn't signed in now sees a Sign in link instead of a blank page, so you can always find your way in. It still shows nothing about your site.
Tables written in Markdown (with | columns) now show as real tables on your pages and in the light copies agents read.
Assistants can now skip re-reading the site guide they already have, which saves them about 13 KB on each repeat site_state call. Reconnect your assistant to get it. Nothing changes if you don't.
Self-hosters and operators can switch on ready-made copies of public pages (off by default). Every change you approve clears the stored copies at once, and nothing private is ever stored.
Approving a change takes no more database work than before.
Your site is now cheaper and easier for AI agents to read: an agent that comes back to a page that hasn't changed gets a tiny "nothing changed" answer instead of the whole page again.
Every public page has a light text copy for agents at <page>/index.md, and the site has a short /llms.txt map of its pages, built only from what you published.
Pages now carry structured facts (business, people, events, offers) for search engines and agents, taken from what the page already shows.
AI-training crawlers are allowed by default; you can switch that off, and your site then says so itself. Search and assistants acting for a person are not affected.
On request your assistant can tell you roughly how many visits came from search crawlers, training crawlers and agents acting for people. Counts only; nothing about visitors is stored.
Photos are now re-checked instead of cached for a year, so a removed photo can't linger in a cache. A private site still shows nothing to anyone signed out.
A site can now have up to 64 streams (it was 8).
Each stream can list its entries newest first or by title.
New, off until you turn it on: one archive page of every entry by date, which visitors can filter by tag and by stream.
If you move back to an older version, a site with more than 8 streams keeps working: it shows the first 8, and nothing you approved is lost when you return.
New, off until you turn it on: an alert on your phone or computer when your assistant sends something for your approval. Turn it on in Review, once per device.
Alerts are a nudge, not a guarantee. Phones and browsers can delay or drop them. Your assistant still sends you the link.
On iPhone, alerts need iOS 16.4 or later and a Home Screen install: Share → Add to Home Screen → open from the icon → turn alerts on.
The Home Screen app now starts at sign-in, then Review, so it works on a private site too, and tapping an alert opens Review in the window you already have open.
When you're signed in, every page of your site shows a Review button at the bottom, because the Home Screen app has no address bar. Visitors and readers never see it.
Assistant apps that run in a browser can now connect to your site. Other websites still can't.
A private site now tells hosting networks not to alter its pages, so tools like Cloudflare's automatic analytics can't add anything to them, and the blank page shown to visitors blocks any script.
Assistants starting a brand-new site are told to create its site settings first, then change them later.

New for older sites: your assistant can check whether published photos still carry the location they were taken at, and replace them with clean copies you approve. Copies already downloaded by others can't be recalled.
Connecting your assistant now works from the browser inside a phone app, where approving the connection used to fail with "This authorization was not started in this browser".
Nothing else changes: you are still the only one who can approve a connection, with your passkey.
Your site can now be private: once you approve it, visitors see a blank page, and only people with a passkey you invited can read it.
Invite readers from the Readers page; each invitation works once for seven days, and you can remove anyone at any time.
If you lose every device, a recovery link from your hosting account lets you sign in again and shuts out your old passkeys.
A new Playbook look for how-to guides: a contents page, numbered steps, 'If something breaks' pages, and clean printing.
The Listing look now shows its highlights only on the home page and the listing itself.
Before rolling a private site back to an older release, your assistant will warn you that it would make the site public.
Photos you add no longer keep the location where they were taken, and photos are shrunk before upload unless you choose to keep the original.
Your site can play videos and tours from sources you approve, right on the page.
A new Listing look for selling one property: a big photo, price and stats, a gallery, tours, open house, contact and an optional brokerage line.
Your site now has a sitemap, phone numbers in your pages can be tapped to call, and adding many photos is quicker.
Going back to the previous release is safe even after you use the new features.
Reconnect your assistant after updating so it sees the new tools.
The Setting up your assistant guide links Grok Bot's ready-made Porchsite template.
The guides and your site's assistant connection say Porchsite throughout.
Before you approve, the preview now shows every page of your site, not just the home page.
An assistant can't connect to a site until its owner has claimed it, and the site says so instead of half-connecting.
The setup page shows which site you're claiming and what the name is for.
Reconnect your assistant after updating so it sees the clearer site check.
Setting up your assistant now covers Grok Bot, the Claude app, ChatGPT and Meta AI by name.
Assistants tell you which look and colours they picked for your site, and what else you could have.
A new guide, Setting up your assistant, shows how to get the most out of the assistant app you already use with Porchsite.
Lost your setup link? Your site's setup page now tells you how to get a new one.
Assistants that talk to your site from their own code get plain answers, and the look checklist names exactly what still needs work.
The install guide gives assistants the right Cloudflare token link for a brand-new account.
The event look shows ordinary posts that sit alongside your events, instead of leaving them off the home page.
A new assistant key now reminds you to put it in your assistant's settings, never in a chat.
The one-page installer shows the claim link once your new address really works, without upsetting your browser.
The one-page installer is smoother on a brand-new Cloudflare account: it asks for everything up front and only shows the claim link once the new address works.
New sites can be installed from one page, get.porchsite.dev/install/, for assistants that can't use Cloudflare themselves.
An assistant that can't reach your site at all can hand you one file with everything it wrote; upload it from your review page and it's checked and waits for your approval like any other change.

An assistant that can't connect with a sign-in can use a key instead: make one for it on your Assistants page and put it in its secret field. It can only draft, like any assistant, and you can revoke it there.
Assistants can send a picture they have as a file straight to your site, instead of asking you to upload it.
Reconnect your assistant after updating so it sees the new picture tool.
A shared journal entry now shows its photo with its title in large type across it, so a link on X reads as the article, not just a picture.
Your browser makes these cards when you open your review page or approve something; older entries get theirs the next time you open it.
Your assistant has a new check, site_check: before it asks for your approval it can find links on your site that lead nowhere and sections with nothing in them.
The menu only shows sections that have something in them.
Reconnect your assistant after updating so it sees the new check.
The install guide names the Cloudflare connector that can do the whole install, and says to put content in only through the site's own tools.
Every release file also has a copy on GitHub, for assistants whose network can't reach get.porchsite.dev.
Porchsite is open source: both editions, the looks and the spec are on GitHub (github.com/iXanadu/porchsite), and this is the first release built from the public code.
The personal-homepage look's project filter works on any site, whatever its projects section is called.
Sample sites use made-up phone numbers, places and handles.
Connecting an assistant: if you have to sign in first, you now land back on the Allow screen instead of your review page.
The install guide asks your person about the site's name and address before anything is made, and never takes the old address away before their passkey works at the new one.
The install guide forbids changing the site's code (only a release's own file is ever uploaded) and says to send finished work as one approval request.
A big review (30 changes or more) opens and publishes in about the same time as a small one; it used to sit for many seconds and look stuck.
Pressing Approve now says at once that it's publishing, and can't be pressed twice; the same for sending back, saving your choices and putting the site back.
The install guide ends by helping your person pick a look that fits their site.
You can change any of your look's own words ("Back to top", the not-found page, opening hours), for example into another language, and say what kind a card group is: FAQ, steps, reviews or a list.
Your review page now says when your assistant has changes it hasn't sent you, and no longer shows a field as changed when only a default was filled in.
Visitor numbers older than 90 days are kept as monthly totals, and sites on the built-in look are counted too.
Putting the site back to an early version keeps your site's text; shared archive pages show their newest cover photo.
Passkey sign-in refuses a bad answer cleanly instead of erroring, and every connected app must use the secure code exchange (PKCE).
Quick checks of a page (HEAD requests) now get the same answer as a visit; some pages wrongly said not found.
The update guide is clearer, from its first real run: it lists every database change so a site that skipped releases knows what it's missing.
Your site now tells your assistant when a newer Porchsite is out, and your review page shows one quiet line about it. Nothing ever updates by itself.
Every release now lists its changes in plain words, says if it's a security fix, and can always be rolled back by putting the previous version back.
The review page shows what changed: the old wording next to the new, open by default.
Long text shows only the words that changed, not two full copies.
Nothing changes on sites themselves; a public form to ask for a feature or report a problem opened at porchsite.dev/ask.
The owner claims a new site from a link (/setup?code=...), with the code already filled in.
Setup codes can be issued after install, work once and expire; claiming the site ends them all.
Needs one new database file (0012) before the new site code.
Fixed: on Cloudflare, an owner page that should say 'not found' or 'link already used' showed a server error instead.
A site's shared looks report whether their maker was credited.
Richer writing: code blocks, nested lists, emphasis, smaller headings and line breaks, rendered the same way in both editions.
Shared looks can credit their maker by X handle, once the curator has checked it.
Sites can be moved over from the older engine (server edition).
The owner (or assistant) can choose a page's address; the old address keeps working and sends visitors on.
The guides are readable as web pages at /docs.
Needs one new database file (0011) before the new site code.
Cards can be public, a mention (name only) or private (never shown, and its name refused in anything public).
Visitor counts without cookies or stored addresses, at /review/stats; the assistant gets a site_stats tool.
The owner can write and publish a page directly at /review/write.
Site history at /review/history: put the whole site back as it was on an earlier day.
Adds a tool: reconnect the assistant. Needs one new database file (0010) before the new site code.
Nothing changes on sites; the self-hosting guide says plainly what the server edition can and can't do yet.
Nothing changes on sites; a self-hosting guide for assistants helping a developer.
Looks credit their authors in the footer.
Demo sites for every look serve their feeds and tag pages.
The product-page look: inner pages read as pages, not as posts.
Every answer from the site names the release it runs (the X-Porchsite-Release header, and release in site_state).
The install guide now deletes the setup code once the site is claimed, and checks for it when updating.
The product-page look: an entry's cover is small spot art, not a screen-sized square.
The review page explains changes in plain words, with one Approve and publish button.
Fixed: the preview could come out unstyled before the first approval or a change of look.
The site code is 40% smaller.
Install guide fixes found while installing a real site.
The theme catalog and downloads moved to get.porchsite.dev.
Eight new looks: event, group, local business, menu, services, catalogue, portfolio and link page.
Contact details, opening hours, notices, buttons and events on the page.
An assistant can share a look it made for review (theme_submit).
Adds a tool: reconnect the assistant. Needs one new database file (0009).
An assistant can make a private look just for its own site.
Adds a tool: reconnect the assistant. Needs one new database file (0008).
Nothing changes on sites; tools for people making looks.
When no look fits, the assistant can ask for one privately (theme_request).
Adds a tool: reconnect the assistant. Needs one new database file (0007).
Looks are named for what the site is for (product-page, personal-homepage).
The owner can see the site as it will look before approving.
The theme catalog shows each look at phone and desktop width.
Looks install from a catalog, and each says what words and pictures it needs.
Adds tools: reconnect the assistant.
www.<domain> sends visitors to <domain>, so a passkey works at one address.
Every released version stays downloadable.
Ships database file 0006 (installed looks) ahead of the theme catalog that uses it; apply it like any other.
Nothing changes on sites (bookkeeping only).
The first archived release: content, review and approval, passkeys, images and photo uploads.
The site's mark (favicon) and share picture.

private_site_rollback: Private sites require the minimum release reported by private_floor. The documented rollback check stops and warns for an older target or unknown state, and proceeds only after explicit owner confirmation. Dashboard rollback, direct upload with the hosting API key, old database restore and a hostile assistant holding the key can expose a private site; prevention is not claimed.
